question: Why does the rule "A function does one thing if you can't meaningfully extract another from it" matter in a code review?

expected_rule_sections.heading: A function does one thing if you can't meaningfully extract another from it
heading_path: Clean Code, Chapter 10: One Thing, PR review rules
A function does one thing if you can't meaningfully extract another from it

relevant_concepts: A function does one thing if you can't meaningfully extract another from it

The test for "one thing" is practical: if you can split a function into two meaningful pieces, it did two things. So extract until you can't meaningfully extract any more, or at least consider every extraction. Most functions end up a few lines long, and typical extractions are the bodies of `if/else` and loops and their predicates, so statements read like prose.

question: What review guidance applies to "Every large function hides a class"?

expected_rule_sections.heading: Every large function hides a class
heading_path: Clean Code, Chapter 10: One Thing, PR review rules
Every large function hides a class

relevant_concepts: Every large function hides a class

A group of methods that manipulate a set of variables is a class. Every large function is hiding one (or more): its locals should be fields, and its indented regions should be methods. Temporarily promoting locals to fields breaks encapsulation but lets you extract, and letting helpers share fields is sometimes cleaner than passing arguments.

question: Why does the rule "Move methods to the class whose data they use" matter in a code review?

expected_rule_sections.heading: Move methods to the class whose data they use
heading_path: Clean Code, Chapter 10: One Thing, PR review rules
Move methods to the class whose data they use

relevant_concepts: Move methods to the class whose data they use

After extraction it becomes clear which code doesn't belong in its class. In the video store example, the amount and points calculations mainly used the rental, so they moved to `Rental`, and the tests passed unchanged because their design tolerated the change. Moving logic to the class that owns the data takes business rules out of a class that was merely holding them.

UI strings are volatile, because someone can change a heading's wording on a whim, and then every test built on them breaks. Test the format once, and have the other tests check the values being computed.
